title: Triple IPA Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Triple IPA explained: the strongest tier of IPA, how it differs from a double IPA, what it tastes like and how to drink it sensibly.
teaser: Above the double IPA sits the triple: 10% ABV or more, loaded with hops and best shared in small pours.
standfirst: Triple IPA is the label brewers use for the strongest, most heavily hopped IPAs, usually around 10% ABV and above. It is not a formal style so much as a step up the ladder. Here is what to expect and how to taste one well.
sections:
IPA comes in tiers. A standard IPA sits around 5.5 to 7.5% ABV. A double or imperial IPA pushes to roughly 7.5 to 10%. Triple IPA is the name brewers use for beers above that, usually from about 10% up to 12% or more.

Unlike West Coast or New England IPA, triple IPA is not a separate category in the main style guidelines. Most competitions would judge one as a double IPA or a specialty beer. The name is a market label that tells you to expect more of everything: more malt, more alcohol, more hops. Our guide to double IPA covers the tier below.

A good triple IPA is intensely aromatic and surprisingly drinkable for its strength. Expect:

  • A huge hop aroma: citrus, pine, tropical fruit, resin, depending on the hops.
  • A firm malt backbone, often with a light honey or caramel sweetness.
  • Noticeable alcohol warmth, which should be smooth rather than hot.
  • High bitterness, though often softened by residual sweetness.

Colour runs from gold to deep amber. Some are clear in the West Coast tradition, others hazy in the New England tradition. The base style shapes texture and bitterness, while strength shapes body and warmth.

Making a clean 11% IPA is hard. The wort is very rich, which stresses yeast. Brewers often add simple sugar, such as dextrose, to raise strength without adding body, so the beer finishes drier and does not feel syrupy.

Yeast health is everything. Strong worts need generous pitching, plenty of oxygen at the start, good nutrients and careful temperature control. Without those, fermentation can stall sweet or throw harsh, solventy alcohols called fusel alcohols. The hop load is also enormous, which means significant beer loss to hop absorption. A triple IPA is one of the most expensive beers a brewery can make per litre.
Hot alcohol is the main fault

The fault to watch for in any strong beer is hot alcohol: a burning, solvent-like heat in the throat. It usually comes from fermenting too warm, especially in the first few days. A well-made triple IPA carries its alcohol as warmth and roundness. A poorly made one tastes like hop-flavoured spirit.

In India, temperature control is the deciding factor. A fermenter left to rise towards 25 °C in a warm brewhouse will produce more fusel alcohol than one held near 18 to 19 °C. When you taste a triple IPA, ask whether the alcohol feels smooth or sharp. That tells you a lot about how carefully it was brewed.

Like any IPA, triple IPA is best fresh. Hop aroma fades within weeks, especially if the beer is warm. Its strength does not protect the hops. As aroma fades, malt sweetness and alcohol become more prominent and the beer starts to taste heavy.

Check the packaging date and buy the freshest you can find. Keep it cold until you drink it. Our guide to fresh versus stale IPA shows how to spot a beer that has lost its hops.

A 440 ml can of 11% beer contains nearly as much alcohol as three 330 ml beers at 5%. Treat triple IPA like a strong wine, not a session beer.

  • Share one can or bottle between two or three people.
  • Pour small measures, around 100 to 150 ml, into a tulip or snifter.
  • Serve at about 8 to 12 °C, slightly warmer than a standard IPA, so the aroma opens.
  • Drink water alongside, eat something and never drive afterwards.

Small pours also make tasting better. Your palate tires quickly with intense hops and alcohol. Our guide to tasting strong beers covers pacing in more detail.
Food that stands up to it

Triple IPA overwhelms delicate food. Choose dishes with strong flavours and some richness:

  • Blue cheese, aged cheddar or a sharp hard cheese.
  • Rich, spiced meats such as a Hyderabadi mutton biryani or seekh kebabs.
  • Carrot cake or a spiced dessert.

Be careful with very hot chilli. Alcohol and hop bitterness both amplify heat, so a fiery vindaloo with a triple IPA can be punishing.

When tasting a triple IPA, separate the layers. First smell the hops and try to name the fruit or resin. Then sip and notice the malt sweetness. Finally, judge the alcohol: is it warm and round or sharp and hot? Compare it, if you can, with a double IPA and a standard IPA from the same brewery. The difference shows you how strength changes balance.

Your first step: next time you see a triple IPA, split it with a friend in small pours and judge whether the alcohol tastes smooth or hot.
faqs: How strong is a triple IPA?
Usually around 10% ABV and above, stronger than a double IPA, which typically sits around 7.5 to 10%.
Is triple IPA an official beer style?
Not in the main style guidelines. It is a market label for the strongest IPAs. Competitions usually judge them as double IPAs or specialty beers.
How should I serve triple IPA?
In small pours of 100 to 150 ml at about 8 to 12 °C, shared between two or three people, with water alongside.
